strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment concern: capability-oriented adaptation can degrade agent safety. Organizing the investigation around model, memory, tool, and workflow evolution provides a useful empirical framework.

The evaluation spans multiple established agent frameworks, model families, and safety benchmarks. Some effects are substantial: SE-Agent’s RedCode attack success rate increases from 0.6% to 20.6%, and AFlow’s increases from 54.4% to 83.1%.

The appendix provides valuable supporting evidence, including task-performance improvements, an RL-versus-SFT comparison, longitudinal observations, and human validation of selected judgments. Tool-evaluation agreement of Cohen’s kappa 0.72 and 0.82 strengthens confidence in those annotations.
Preliminary mitigations offer actionable findings. In particular, memory prompting reduces harmful generation while preserving the reported 60% SWE-Bench resolution rate on the evaluated subset.
weaknesses: The central claim of a distinct, spontaneously emerging safety phenomenon is broader than the evidence supports. The experiments combine benign fine-tuning degradation, biased in-context learning, insecure code reuse, malicious repository ingestion, and ensemble selection. The taxonomy is useful, but the paper does not sufficiently establish what distinguishes these mechanisms from existing safety failures beyond their occurrence within an adaptation pipeline.

The memory experiments contain substantial construction bias. The main AgentNet evaluation uses 40 manually authored cases with deliberately skewed feedback rather than naturally accumulated experience. More seriously, Appendix C.2.2 presents an evaluation-agent prompt that explicitly rewards lying and penalizes honesty, despite describing the dynamic experiment as customer-service refund interactions. This mismatch impedes reproduction and weakens the claim that the observed drift arises without deliberately harmful environmental incentives.

Critical counterfactual controls are missing. Tool reuse is not compared with solving the same security-sensitive task from scratch; evolved workflows are not compared with a fixed, compute-matched three-sample ensemble; and the SE-Agent memory evaluation changes both the memory and the surrounding instructions. Consequently, the experiments establish failures in evolved configurations more convincingly than they isolate risks specifically introduced by evolution.

The external-tool experiment is particularly weak evidence for spontaneous misevolution: repositories are intentionally seeded with malicious code, and the packaging prompt instructs models to mainly read the README rather than the code. Refusal rises from approximately 3–7% to approximately 69% when security checking is requested, indicating considerable sensitivity to task framing. There is no clean-repository control measuring false refusals or execution-based demonstration that the packaged feature activates the injected behavior.

The model experiments do not adequately distinguish lost safety alignment from improved ability to answer harmful requests. Much of the Absolute-Zero evaluation begins with base models rather than safety-aligned instruction models. Capability gains, chat-template effects, and nonresponsive outputs require stronger controls before interpreting lower safe rates as erosion of an initial alignment mechanism. The SFT comparison is informative but does not establish optimization pressure as the primary cause without matched training budgets.

Evidence for generality and temporal dynamics remains limited: tool creation uses 25 cases, static memory evaluation has only 10 cases per domain, and workflow optimization examines one backbone and one resulting workflow. Repeated runs are reported for static memory evaluation, but comparable uncertainty estimates and independent evolution seeds are absent for most experiments. The abrupt-collapse claim rests on a narrow simulated trajectory.

Several reporting issues further weaken confidence. Workflow selection is described as using the HumanEval test set, while the appendix reports validation performance without clearly resolving the split protocol. The introduction’s claim of vulnerabilities in over 76% of tool cases is inconsistent with Table 2, whose maximum is 76% and whose mean is 65.5%. These issues, together with the missing controls, prevent the otherwise useful empirical survey from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment concern: improvements in task performance can coincide with deteriorating safety. Organizing the investigation around model, memory, tool, and workflow evolution provides a useful framework.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning established agent frameworks, multiple model families, and several safety benchmarks. Particularly notable results include SE-Agent’s refusal rate falling from 99.4% to 54.4% and AFlow’s attack success rate increasing from 54.4% to 83.1%.

The appendices strengthen the evidence with task-performance comparisons, an RL-versus-SFT ablation, longitudinal measurements, and human validation of selected LLM judgments. Tool-evaluation agreement with human annotators reaches Cohen’s kappa of 0.72 and 0.82 for two models.

Preliminary mitigations provide useful practical evidence. Explicit security instructions substantially improve malicious-tool detection, while the memory intervention improves safety without reducing the reported SWE-Bench resolution rate.
weaknesses: The central framing exceeds the evidence. The manuscript emphasizes spontaneous, internally generated risks without deliberate exposure to unsafe data, but major experiments use manually biased memories or deliberately injected malicious repositories. These establish vulnerabilities under constructed conditions, rather than the prevalence of spontaneous misevolution. The distinction from benign fine-tuning degradation, memory poisoning, reward misspecification, and insecure code reuse needs sharper empirical support.

The external-tool experiment has a consequential prompt confound (Appendix C.3.2): agents are explicitly told to mainly read the README rather than the code and to package the entire project. Very low refusal under these instructions does not establish a general inability to detect malicious tools. Detection rises to approximately 69% with a security instruction. There are also no clean-repository controls to measure false positives, and the judge prompt asks about any security consideration rather than directly verifying the claimed refusal outcome or successful detection of the injected behavior.

The memory evidence insufficiently separates autonomous learning from imposed feedback bias. Most reward-hacking results use 40 manually constructed cases with six selected experiences each. More seriously, Appendix C.2.2 presents a customer-service/refund simulation but supplies an evaluator prompt for a sales scenario that explicitly rewards lying and penalizes honesty. Whether this reflects the actual experiment or a documentation error, it prevents reproduction and interpretation of the longitudinal result.

Controls needed to attribute the regressions specifically to evolution are missing. Tool reuse lacks a fresh-generation baseline on the same security-sensitive tasks. Workflow evolution lacks a compute-matched fixed ensemble or random-selection control. SE-Agent’s memory comparison changes both the stored content and the surrounding instructions, without neutral-memory or instruction-only controls. The observed differences therefore do not isolate the proposed mechanisms.

The interpretation of model results as erosion of safety alignment requires more care. Absolute-Zero experiments start from Base/Coder checkpoints rather than explicitly safety-aligned instruction models, and increased harmful-task competence can lower measured safe rates without demonstrating loss of an existing refusal policy. The SFT ablation is useful but does not resolve this distinction; matched capability and prompt-format controls would strengthen the claim.

Statistical support is uneven. The static memory study includes three runs, but the dynamic collapse claim rests on a narrowly evaluated trajectory with ten test queries, and tool creation uses only 25 curated cases. Repeated evolutionary runs and uncertainty estimates are needed before generalizing the temporal patterns as cumulative model degradation versus abrupt memory collapse.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence. The introduction claims vulnerable tool generation and reuse in over 76% of cases, whereas Table 2 reports 56–76% overall unsafe rates and distinguishes tool vulnerabilities from unsafe application flows. Workflow selection is described as using the HumanEval test set, while Appendix D.7 reports validation-set performance; the split and selection protocol need clarification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment concern: improvements in agent capability can accompany deteriorating safety. Organizing the investigation around model, memory, tool, and workflow evolution provides a useful framework.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning several existing agent frameworks, multiple model families, and established safety benchmarks. The SE-Agent memory experiment is particularly compelling: refusal falls from 99.4% to 54.4%, while attack success increases from 0.6% to 20.6%.

The appendices strengthen the study with capability measurements, an RL-versus-SFT comparison, detailed prompts, and human validation of selected evaluations. The reported tool-evaluation agreement provides useful support for the automated judgments.
Preliminary mitigations offer actionable evidence. For example, the memory intervention reduces harmful behavior while preserving the reported 60% SWE-Bench resolution rate on the evaluated subset.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately establish misevolution as a distinct phenomenon beyond known benign-fine-tuning degradation, reward misspecification, contextual conditioning, and software supply-chain risks. Appendix D.8 explicitly connects the model findings to benign fine-tuning and finds greater degradation under SFT. The contribution is primarily a broad empirical synthesis, but the novelty claims are stronger than this positioning supports.

The memory reward-hacking experiments predominantly use 40 manually constructed cases with deliberately biased histories. These establish susceptibility to biased context, rather than the prevalence of spontaneously emerging failures. The dynamic experiment is also difficult to reproduce: Appendix C.2.2 describes a customer-service simulation, but its supplied evaluator prompt concerns drone sales and explicitly rewards lying. This mismatch needs resolution, alongside balanced-feedback controls and repeated independent trajectories.

The external-tool experiment is strongly confounded by its instructions. Appendix C.3.2 tells agents to prioritize the README over source code and package the entire project. The near-universal failure to reject malicious repositories therefore does not establish an intrinsic inability to detect threats; explicit security instructions raise rejection to approximately 69% for two models. Moreover, the judge asks whether any security issue or security design was considered, which does not cleanly operationalize the reported Refusal Rate. Clean repositories and verified downstream execution outcomes are missing.

Important causal controls are absent. Tool reuse is not compared with solving the second task from scratch; memory augmentation changes both context and instructions without matched prompt controls; and the evolved workflow is not compared with a fixed, compute-matched three-sample ensemble. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate which additional risks arise from evolution itself rather than ordinary insecure generation, prompting, or increased sampling.

Claims of pervasive and characteristic temporal behavior exceed the supporting longitudinal evidence. Memory collapse is illustrated using one backbone, one service scenario, and ten evaluation queries; workflow evolution uses one backbone and one optimization setting. Three repetitions of the static memory experiment and selected human checks are helpful, but do not establish stability across independent evolutionary runs or support broad prevalence estimates from curated stress tests.

Several interpretations and reporting choices need tightening. Absolute-Zero starts from Base/Coder checkpoints, so reduced safe-output rates do not by themselves demonstrate erosion of established safety alignment. Workflow selection is described as using the HumanEval test set, while Appendix D.7 reports validation performance, leaving the selection protocol unclear. Most mitigations also lack capability trade-off measurements. These issues limit confidence in the paper's central explanations despite the useful observed failures.
